title: Your Body, and How You Feel
overview:
Name the parts of your body.
Say how you feel.
Say where it hurts.
Ask for help.
functions: Name the parts of your body
Say how you feel: tired, ill, happy, sad
Understand a person who asks how you are
learningPath: Words: your body, and how you feel.
Patterns: my head hurts, and I need help.
Say where it hurts. Record it.
Write four lines about a bad day.
Practice and quiz. Check your answers.
lectureScript:
This is Unit 11. This one is important.
If you are ill, you must be able to say so.
First, your body. Point as you listen.
Your head. Your hand. Your arm.
Your leg. Your eye. Your ear. Your foot.
Say them with me. Head. Hand. Arm.
Leg. Eye. Ear. Foot.
And the word for all of it: body.
Now, how you feel.
I am tired. I am ill.
I am happy. I am sad.
Say them with me. Tired. Ill. Happy. Sad.
Remember: you ARE tired. Not you have tired.
Now the most useful sentence today.
My head hurts.
Say it with me. My head hurts.
My arm hurts. My leg hurts.
Any part of your body. Say it hurts.
Or say: I have a pain in my arm.
Both are right. The short one is easier.
Last, getting help.
Help, please.
I need a doctor.
Where is the hospital?
Say them with me. Help, please. I need a doctor.
Learn those three. They are for a bad day.
That is Unit 11. Say it out loud many times.

She has a pain in her head.

grammar.title: My head hurts
grammar.explanation:
The most useful sentence in this unit.
Two words and a body part.
It works for every part of you.
grammar.rule:
My head hurts.
My arm hurts.
My leg hurts.
My ear hurts.

More than one part:
My feet hurt.   (no s)
My eyes hurt.
grammar.workedExample:
Your arm is painful.
1. Start with my.
2. Then the part: arm.
3. Then hurts.
4. Say: My arm hurts.
5. Point at it while you say it. That always helps.
grammar.mistake:
One part takes hurts.
More than one takes hurt, with no s.
My foot hurts. My feet hurt.
grammar.practice:
Make a sentence.
1. head
2. arm
3. leg
4. ear
5. feet
6. eyes
grammar.answers:
1. My head hurts.
2. My arm hurts.
3. My leg hurts.
4. My ear hurts.
5. My feet hurt.
6. My eyes hurt.
Five or six right? You can tell a doctor where it is.

grammar.title: I am tired, I am ill
grammar.explanation:
Feelings take am, not have.
This is the same rule as hungry in Unit 10.
grammar.rule:
I am tired.
I am ill.
I am happy.
I am sad.
I am better.

Are you tired?
Yes, I am.
No, I am not.
grammar.workedExample:
You did not sleep and you need rest.
1. Tired is a feeling.
2. So use am, not have.
3. Say: I am tired.
4. Add why: I am tired. I did not sleep.
5. Two short lines are enough.
grammar.mistake:
No: I have tired.
Yes: I am tired.
Same for ill, happy, sad and hungry.
grammar.practice:
Write am or have.
1. I ___ tired.
2. I ___ a pain in my arm.
3. I ___ ill.
4. I ___ a headache.
5. I ___ sad.
6. I ___ better today.
grammar.answers:
1. am
2. have
3. am
4. have
5. am
6. am
Five or six right? A pain is a thing, so it takes have.

grammar.title: Two ways to say it hurts
grammar.explanation:
One is shorter. One is what a doctor asks.
Learn the short one first.
grammar.rule:
Short:  My arm hurts.
Longer: I have a pain in my arm.

The doctor asks:
Where does it hurt?
Where is the pain?

You answer: Here. (and point)
grammar.workedExample:
A doctor asks where it hurts.
1. The shortest true answer is best.
2. Point at the place.
3. Say: Here. My arm hurts.
4. Or: I have a pain here.
5. Pointing is not rude. It is clear.
grammar.mistake:
Do not build a long sentence when you are ill.
Here, and a point, is a complete answer.
grammar.practice:
Say it both ways.
1. head
2. arm
3. leg
4. ear
grammar.answers:
1. My head hurts. / I have a pain in my head.
2. My arm hurts. / I have a pain in my arm.
3. My leg hurts. / I have a pain in my leg.
4. My ear hurts. / I have a pain in my ear.
All four? You can describe pain two ways.

grammar.title: Asking for help
grammar.explanation:
Three short sentences for a bad day.
Learn them until you do not have to think.
grammar.rule:
Help, please.
I need a doctor.
Where is the hospital?

And one more:
Can you help me, please?

In a real emergency: Help! Quick!
grammar.workedExample:
You feel very ill in a shop.
1. Do not try to explain everything.
2. Say: Help, please. I am ill.
3. Then: I need a doctor.
4. They will do the rest.
5. Three short sentences are enough.
grammar.mistake:
Do not wait until you can say it well.
Help, please is enough, and it works.
grammar.tip: Short is better when it is urgent.
grammar.practice:
What do you say?
1. You feel very ill. ___
2. You do not know where to go. ___
3. You cannot do it alone. ___
4. It is very bad and you need somebody now. ___
grammar.answers:
1. I am ill. I need a doctor.
2. Where is the hospital?
3. Can you help me, please?
4. Help! Quick!
All four? These are the sentences that matter most in this unit.

readings.title: A Bad Day
readings.setting: A small flat, on a cold morning
readings.passage:
I am ill today.
My head hurts.
My body is hot.
I am very tired.
I do not want food.
I drink water.
I do not go to work.
I stay in bed.
Tomorrow I hope I am better.

readings.title: Where Does It Hurt?
readings.setting: A small room at a clinic
readings.passage:
Good morning. How are you?
Not good. I am ill.
Where does it hurt?
Here. My head hurts.
And my ear.
How long?
Two days.
Take this medicine.
Thank you, doctor.

readings.title: If You Need Help
readings.genre: A sign in a waiting room
readings.passage:
Ill? Sit and wait.
Very ill? Tell the desk now.

In an emergency:
Say: Help. Quick.
The hospital is behind this building.

comprehension.why: Line 5: I do not want food.
Line 7: I do not go to work.

comprehension.q: What does the doctor ask first?
comprehension.why: Line 1: Good morning. How are you?

comprehension.q: You are ill. What do you do?

comprehension.why: The last line of the sign.

speaking.title: Speaking 1 — Point and name
speaking.instructions:
Point at each part of your body and name it.
1. head
2. hand
3. arm
4. leg
5. eye
6. ear
7. foot
Do it two times. The second time, do not read.
Tap the mic. Say all seven.
Check: did you point at each one?
speaking.tutor: Ask the tutor to name a body part. Point at it on yourself.

speaking.title: Speaking 2 — How do you feel?
speaking.instructions:
Say each line out loud.
1. I am tired.
2. I am ill.
3. I am happy.
4. I am sad.
5. I am better today.
6. I am not well.
Tap the mic. Say the six lines.
Check: am in every one?
speaking.tutor: Tell the tutor how you feel today. Ask how it is.

speaking.title: Speaking 3 — Where does it hurt?
speaking.instructions:
Point at a part of your body. Say it hurts.
1. My head hurts.
2. My arm hurts.
3. My leg hurts.
4. My ear hurts.
5. My feet hurt.
6. My eyes hurt.
Tap the mic. Say the six lines.
Check: hurts for one, hurt for more than one?
speaking.tutor: Tell the tutor where it hurts. Point as you say it.

speaking.title: Speaking 4 — Ask for help
speaking.instructions:
These are for a bad day. Say them clearly.
1. Help, please.
2. I am ill.
3. I need a doctor.
4. Where is the hospital?
5. Can you help me, please?
Tap the mic. Say all five.
Tap again. Listen back.
Say them again tomorrow. And the day after.
speaking.tutor: Tell the tutor you are ill and need help. Listen to what it says.

speaking.title: Speaking 5 — How are you?
speaking.instructions:
Read A. Say B.
1. A: How are you? B: I am fine, thank you.
2. A: How are you? B: Not good. I am ill.
3. A: Where does it hurt? B: Here. My head hurts.
4. A: I am sorry. B: Thank you.
Tap the mic. Say the four B lines.
Check: two different answers to the same question?
speaking.tutor: Ask the tutor how it is. Answer when it asks you.

speaking.title: Speaking 6 — Hurt and heart
speaking.instructions:
Two words that look close. Listen.
hurt ... heart ... hurt ... heart
They are not the same.
Now these body words.
head ... hand ... arm ... ear
The h at the start is a breath.
Tap the mic. Say: My head hurts. My hand hurts.
Check: can you hear the h?
speaking.tutor: Ask the tutor to say hurt and heart. Say which one you heard.

writing.title: Writing 1 — How I feel today
writing.prompt:
Write four lines.
Say how you feel and why.
Use I am in each line.
writing.model:
I am tired today.
I did not sleep well.
My head hurts a little.
But I am happy to be here.
writing.criteria:
Four lines.
I am in at least three of them.
Each line starts with a capital.
Each line ends with a full stop.
writing.extension: Add one line about how you feel tomorrow.

writing.title: Writing 2 — A note for the doctor
writing.prompt:
Write four short lines for a doctor.
Say what hurts and how long.
writing.model:
I am ill.
My head hurts.
My ear hurts too.
It is two days now.
writing.criteria:
Four lines.
At least one says what hurts.
At least one says how long.
Every line is short and clear.
writing.support: Write two lines only: what hurts, and how long.
writing.extension: Add a line saying what medicine you take.

activities.title: Practice 1 — Name the part
activities.instructions:
What is it?
1. You see with it. ___
2. You hear with it. ___
3. You hold things with it. ___
4. You walk on it. ___
5. It is at the top of you. ___
6. It is at the end of your leg. ___
7. From your shoulder to your hand. ___
8. All of you. ___
activities.answers:
1. eye
2. ear
3. hand
4. leg (or foot)
5. head
6. foot
7. arm
8. body
Six or more right: good.
activities.solo: Point at each one as you answer.

activities.title: Practice 2 — Am or have
activities.instructions:
Write am or have.
1. I ___ tired.
2. I ___ a pain in my arm.
3. I ___ ill.
4. I ___ a headache.
5. I ___ sad.
6. I ___ better today.
activities.answers:
1. am
2. have
3. am
4. have
5. am
6. am
Five or six right: good. A pain is a thing, so have.

activities.title: Practice 3 — Say where it hurts
activities.instructions:
Make a sentence for each one.
1. head
2. arm
3. leg
4. ear
5. feet
6. eyes
activities.answers:
1. My head hurts.
2. My arm hurts.
3. My leg hurts.
4. My ear hurts.
5. My feet hurt.
6. My eyes hurt.
Five or six right: good. Feet and eyes take hurt, with no s.
activities.solo: Say each one out loud and point.

activities.title: Practice 4 — What do you say?
activities.instructions:
Choose the best sentence.
1. You feel very ill. ___
2. You do not know where to go. ___
3. You cannot do it alone. ___
4. It is very bad and urgent. ___
5. A doctor asks where. ___
activities.answers:
1. I am ill. I need a doctor.
2. Where is the hospital?
3. Can you help me, please?
4. Help! Quick!
5. Here. My head hurts. (and point)
Four or five right: you can ask for help.
activities.solo: Say your answers out loud first.

activities.title: Practice 5 — How are you?
activities.instructions:
Answer each one about yourself.
1. How are you today?
2. Are you tired?
3. Does anything hurt?
4. Are you happy today?
5. Are you better than yesterday?
activities.answers:
Any true answer is right.
Check: did you use am for the feelings?
Did you answer in a whole sentence?
Four or five answered: good.
activities.solo: Record all five, then listen back.

activities.title: Practice 6 — Read the sign
activities.instructions:
Read If You Need Help again.
1. You are ill. What do you do?
2. You are very ill. What do you do?
3. What two words do you say in an emergency?
4. Where is the hospital?
5. Do you wait if you are very ill?
activities.answers:
1. Sit and wait
2. Tell the desk now
3. Help. Quick.
4. Behind this building
5. No
Four or five right: you can read a sign that matters.
activities.solo: Read it, then answer without looking.

quizzes.q: You see with it. It is your ___.
quizzes.why: You see with your eye and hear with your ear.

quizzes.q: You hear with it. It is your ___.
More than one foot is two ___.
quizzes.why: Foot becomes feet, like man becomes men.

quizzes.q: You need to sleep. You say: I ___ tired.
Which one is a feeling, not a thing?
quizzes.why: Ill is a feeling and takes am. A pain is a thing and takes have.

quizzes.q: Your head is painful. You say: My head ___.
quizzes.why: One part takes hurts. More than one takes hurt.

quizzes.q: Your feet are painful. You say: My feet ___.
quizzes.why: Feet is more than one, so hurt with no s.

quizzes.q: You feel very ill. What is the most useful thing to say?
quizzes.why: Short and clear is best when you are ill.

quizzes.q: You cannot do it alone. You say ___.
quizzes.why: Asking for help directly is faster than waiting.

quizzes.q: Where do doctors work? At the ___.
quizzes.why: A hospital is the big building where doctors work.

quizzes.q: A person asks: How are you? A good answer is ___.
quizzes.why: How are you asks about your health or your feelings.

quizzes.q: You are less ill than yesterday. You say: I am ___.
quizzes.why: Better means less bad than before.

teacherNotes.note: Every pattern card has a worked example, every practice has a key, and every speaking task ends with record, listen back, check.

teacherNotes.type: This is the survival unit of the level
teacherNotes.note: A comparison of this course against Interchange Intro found health to be its largest gap. At Pre-A1 the minimum is being able to point at a part of the body, say it hurts, and ask for help. Everything else in the unit is around those three. If time runs short, keep Pattern 1 and Pattern 4 and drop the rest.

teacherNotes.type: Pointing is part of the language here
teacherNotes.note: A learner who points and says here has communicated perfectly. Teach the point as part of the sentence rather than as a failure to find words, and a learner in real pain will still be understood.

teacherNotes.type: Learn the three help sentences to automatic
teacherNotes.note: Help, please. I need a doctor. Where is the hospital? These need to come out without thinking, because the day they are needed is the day thinking is hardest. Come back to Speaking 4 in later units, not just this one.
Same rule as hungry in Unit 10, and it is worth naming the link out loud: ill, tired, happy, sad, hungry and thirsty all take am. A pain and a headache are things, so they take have.

selfAssessment.statement: I can name the parts of my body.
I can say how I feel.
I can say where it hurts.
I can say I need a doctor.
I can answer when you ask how I am.

assignment.title: Say where it hurts, and ask for help
assignment.instructions:
Two parts.
1. Record yourself. Name six parts of your body.
Then say three of these: My head hurts. I am ill. I need a doctor.
Say them slowly and clearly.
2. Write four short lines for a doctor.
Say what hurts and how long.
Listen back before you finish.
assignment.submissionType: Audio recording and a written page
